$about: 2026-08-06: ten open failures re-run before anything was changed - five gates that passed where they had to fail, five claims the tree makes about itself. Every case was reproduced against the shipped code first, on the rule that a finding is open only while it still reproduces. Two did not reproduce as recorded: DOC-15 was closed by a commit on 2026-08-04 and is proved closed here rather than re-fixed, and GATE-32's recorded instances (all directory-shaped) are closed while the same coincidence survives one entry-shape over. The observations keep the earlier rounds' target labels so they supersede those findings on the punch list; each evidence field states which tree the run was executed against. The fix for all ten is pull request #46, open and deliberately unmerged at the time of writing - sibling pull requests touch the same generated files and integration order is handled centrally.

observations.evidence: Reproduced before anything was changed. A fixture carrying `docs/personas.md` with a roster and one capability spec declaring `**Spec tier:** buildable`, `**Serves:**` a roster persona, `**Status:** in-refinement`, and no `## Data contracts` or `## Interface contracts`, run through the shipped guard: `node standard/scripts/spec-structure.mjs --block` printed `spec-structure: OK (1 spec paths)` and exited 0. The sections are marked `buildable: REQUIRED` in `standard/specs/capability-spec.template.md` and nothing read the template - `standard/specs/enforcement.md` even advertised the check ('a spec missing the sections that make it usable at the tier it declares') while no code performed it. Fixed by a fourth check in spec-structure.mjs: a spec declaring `buildable` must carry `## Data contracts`, `## Interface contracts` and `## Acceptance criteria`, each with something under the heading. The same fixture now exits 1 with `missing: ## Data contracts, ## Interface contracts` - naming both, and not naming Acceptance criteria, which it had. Scope was chosen against the failure mode that a guard firing on legitimate shapes gets disabled, and every legitimate shape has its own case in `tools/clarify-gate-test.mjs` (13 new cases, 8 of them pass-direction): the behavioral tier still passes untouched (R9's escape hatch), a section that says 'None - this capability persists nothing' passes, a body opening with a `###` sub-heading counts as filled, `## Acceptance criteria (capture)` satisfies the requirement, and a named sub-spec is held to the tier only when it declares one itself. An empty heading and a heading carrying only the template's own comment both fail, because a dropped heading and an empty one read identically downstream. `Algorithms & rules` is deliberately NOT required: the template conditions it on 'where logic is non-trivial', which no script can judge. A spec declaring no tier at all is WARNED about rather than failed - R9 makes buildable the default, so silence makes the same claim, but failing every undeclared spec in a repo mid-adoption is how a guard gets switched off; deleting the line is therefore not a silent way out. What this does NOT claim: nothing checks that a present section is any good - substance stays the judgment tier. The check found three live instances in this repository's own tree (`tree-guard`, `verify-engine`, `web-surface` each declared buildable with no `## Data contracts`), all three now written from the code rather than waived.

Reproduced as a vocabulary gap, by reading and by running - not against a checkout of bazel, but against a fixture of exactly the shape the case describes (a capability whose implementation is in a repository this one does not own). `standard/scripts/spec-guard.mjs`'s `parseEntry` accepted a glob string or `{ glob, couples }` and refused everything else with the map declared unusable, and neither `standard/specs/capability-map.example.json` nor `standard/specs/enforcement.md` had any provision for external code. So the two available moves were both reported as defects: a glob matching nothing (`--audit`: 'globs that match no file in the tree - the guard is watching nothing') or no map entry at all ('capability specs with no map entry'). Being wrong about an ordinary shape, in a way the author has to route around, is how a map stops being maintained. Fixed by a third entry form, `{ "external": "<repo>", "reason": "<why no glob here reaches it>" }` (ADR-036). Verified live: a fixture with `specs/rules-go/spec.md` and that entry reports `spec-guard --audit: OK (1 capability specs, all mapped; 0 globs, all matching; ...; 1 external binding(s) not enforced here)` plus a per-run note naming the repository and the reason. The hatch is bounded, and each bound has a case in `tools/spec-guard-test.mjs` (6 new cases, 5 of which fail against the unfixed guard): an external entry with no reason is refused with the map unusable; the capability still needs a spec directory here; the named repository claims no local path, so code it might have covered is still reported unclaimed; and a capability holding globs AND an external entry still couples on the globs. What is NOT claimed: nothing verifies the named repository exists, is spelled correctly, or still holds that code - it is a record, not a link that is followed, and ADR-036 says so.

Reproduced by running, not only by reading the script as the 2026-08-04 round did. A fixture built from the current shipped tree, carrying `stack.manifest.json` (technology `node-typescript`, one required entry `package.json`) and `stack.dart-flutter.manifest.json` (technology `dart-flutter`, one required entry `pubspec.yaml`), reported only the first: `stack manifest present: node-typescript`, `FAIL file package.json missing`, and no mention of the second manifest, its technology or its entry anywhere in the output. Drift moved by exactly one against the same fixture's baseline. That is worse than an unsupported case - a repo would read full adoption of a layer that was never measured. Fixed by discovering every root file matching `/^stack(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*)?\.manifest\.json$/`, reading them in filename order, and merging each into the same four arrays; the same fixture now reports both technologies and drift +2 (ADR-037, and one clause added to R20 - the previous round declined to change the contract unilaterally, which was right). Four cases in `tools/self-verify-drift-test.mjs` hold it, three of which fail against the unfixed engine: both stacks count and are both named; two stacks declaring one path are checked once per declaration with the doubling stated rather than collapsed (collapsing means picking a winner between two upstream repos this one does not own); `mystack.manifest.json` is not read as a stack; and an unparseable second manifest is drift naming the file rather than a silent skip. What is NOT claimed: no run was made against a checkout of flutter/flutter, and nothing checks that the filename's technology segment matches the manifest's own `technology` field - both are printed, and a check would fail repos whose stack repo simply named the file differently.

Reproduced exactly as recorded, in a throwaway git repo with one tracked, mapped spec (`specs/booking/`) and one untracked, unmapped directory (`specs/payments/`). Before `git add`: `spec-guard --audit: OK (1 capability specs, all mapped; 1 globs, all matching; 3 files, each claimed by a capability or declared unclaimed)`, exit 0. After `git add`, nothing else changed: `1 problem(s) ... capability specs with no map entry: specs/payments/`, exit 1. Same tree, two answers, and the local one was the wrong one - on exactly the capability the audit exists for, the one somebody just created. Cause confirmed in the source: `listed()` returned `git ls-files` and only fell through to the filesystem walk when git listed nothing at all, so one tracked spec was enough to hide every new directory. Fixed by unioning tracked and untracked (`--others --exclude-standard`), with `node_modules` and `.git` dropped by name so a repo that has not ignored them gets the filesystem fallback's answer rather than thousands of orphans; the fixture now reports the orphan identically before and after staging. Six cases in `tools/spec-guard-test.mjs`, three of which fail against the unfixed guard, and half of them in the direction that matters more here: untracked code inside a capability's globs is claimed rather than unclaimed, ignored build output is not code nobody claims, and a glob whose only matches are untracked is no longer reported as a guard watching nothing - which it was, as a false positive, for the same reason. git's stderr is now discarded in that helper, so a repo with no `.git` gets the fallback instead of four `fatal: not a git repository` lines.

Half of this no longer reproduces and half did. Run first, on a copy of the current tree: the recorded instances are all directory-shaped (kibana's `.claude/skills` symlink at its own 31-skill system, svelte's unrelated skills directory), and deleting `.claude/skills` while planting an unrelated directory at the altPath now reports `FAIL content .agents/skills stands in for .claude/skills but 20 of the standard's 20 are not in it: ...`, drift +1 - closed by the by-name port check, with a case already holding it. The same coincidence one entry-shape over was still open: a `copy` entry for a single FILE, resolved through an `altPath`, was never compared at all. Reproduced by giving `SPEC.md` an altPath of `docs/SPEC.md` in a fixture's manifest, deleting `SPEC.md` and writing one line of unrelated text at the alternate path: `PASS file SPEC.md`, then `···· content SPEC.md resolved through an alternate path - content not compared`, and drift stayed at the baseline. The run said the content was not compared, in a dim note that reads like a pass. Fixed by hashing it like any other copy entry: the same fixture now reports `FAIL content docs/SPEC.md stands in for SPEC.md but its content is not the standard's`. The distinction is deliberate and is in the message - a directory at an alternate path may be a port, a different format by design, which is why it is checked by name; a file may not, because an altPath names a different location for the standard's file rather than permission for a different file. Three cases in `tools/self-verify-drift-test.mjs`, all three failing against the unfixed engine, and two of them in the passing direction: a faithful copy at the alternate path passes and says so, and a repo that deliberately rewrote the file records `{ kind: content }` and stops drifting. The ported-directory case is untouched. Not claimed: the shipped manifest has no single-file copy entry with an altPath today, so this closes an engine hole reachable from a stack manifest or a future entry rather than a live drift in this repository.

The instance the 2026-08-05 re-run found still reproduced and is closed, and the general problem is now held by a guard rather than by a sweep. Verified independently before changing anything: across all 88 entries in every array of `standard/standard.manifest.json`, `since` values remain heterogeneous (0.1.0 x4, 0.2.0 x2, 0.3.0 x5, 0.4.0 x3, 0.5.0 x8, 0.7.2 x2, 1.0.0 x57, unreleased x6), so the original mass-corruption bug does not recur; exactly one value was ahead of `VERSION` - `scripts/lib` declaring `since: "1.0.14"` against a VERSION of 1.0.13. Traced to its commit: `git log -S'"since": "1.0.14"'` gives b2bd46b (2026-08-04, 'fix(spec-guard): match globs that name a top-level directory'), whose own `VERSION` was already 1.0.13 - so the number was a guess at what the next release would be called, added inside an unrelated fix, while every other not-yet-released entry in the same file used the literal `unreleased`. The entry now says `unreleased`. Editing one value does not close the class, so `tools/tree-check.mjs` gained a check over every object in every array: `since` must be `unreleased` or an x.y.z release not ahead of VERSION, compared numerically part by part (as strings `1.0.9` sorts after `1.0.13`, and the ahead-of-VERSION case this exists for would read as fine). Proved in both directions: reintroducing `1.0.14` makes tree-check fail naming the entry, and `node tools/tree-check.mjs --self` runs 11 cases - `unreleased`, the current version, an older release and an older patch that sorts later as a string must pass; the next uncut patch, a future minor, a future major, a two-part version, a release candidate, an unrecognised word and a missing value must fail - wired into this repo's CI beside the tree check. What is still NOT claimed, and the case's own procedure cannot give: that every historical `since` matches `git log --follow`. Most read 1.0.0 because that is when the manifest-tracked shape of the tree began, and chasing pre-manifest renames is not what the field declares. What is now mechanical is the half that can be: no entry may name a release that does not exist.

Reproduced verbatim against the current tree: `grep -n '1\.0\.0'` returns `docs/faq.md:117`, `README.md:67`, `llms.txt:22` and `site/llms.txt:22`, `VERSION` reads 1.0.13, and `docs/facts.json`'s `standard-version` fact covered five surfaces - SPEC.md's header, the method doc, self-verify.mjs's usage line, the landing's version pill and the manifest - none of which is one of those four. Two of the four are what a person or a model reads first about the project. All four now state the real version and are declared as claims, which is the part that lasts: facts-check compares each captured value against `VERSION` and also fails a claim whose pattern matches nothing, so a surface reworded past its own pattern fails rather than dropping quietly out of coverage. Proved in both directions rather than assumed: `standard-version = 1.0.13 - 9 restatement(s) agree` on the corrected tree, and setting README.md back to 1.0.0 gives `FAIL standard-version: README.md says "1.0.0", the source says "1.0.13"` with exit 1. The deployed copy `site/llms.txt` is covered separately from the root file it is generated from, so a root edit that was never regenerated is caught rather than assumed. Cost stated rather than hidden: cutting a release now has to move nine restatements instead of five, and each of the four added was previously free to be wrong.

Reproduced by reading the two workflows side by side, as the case's procedure says: `standard/.github/workflows/spec-guard.yml` had `on:` carrying `pull_request:` and nothing else, while the sibling `standard/.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml` carries `push: branches: [main]` alongside it, with its reasoning written down. So `site/index.html`'s 'CI gates compliance from the first push' described a workflow that never ran on a push - including the very first one, when a repository has no pull requests at all and every file in it is arriving unchecked. Fixed by adding `push: branches: [main]`, matching the sibling exactly, plus a concurrency group. The steps that need two sides adapt rather than break, and each path was run before this shipped: on a push the structure guard reads the whole tree instead of a diff, and the coupling guard diffs against `github.event.before` only when it is set (a first push sends all-zeros) and still resolvable (`git cat-file -e` - a force-push can remove it), otherwise it says so and the full-tree audit is the gate. Simulated all three with the step's own script: all-zeros gives 'No earlier commit to diff against', a real SHA gives `spec-guard: OK` in diff mode, and a vanished SHA falls back rather than dying on a missing ref, which would show the same red as a real violation. `on.push` was added to the entry's `requiredKeys` so a merge that keeps a repo's own pull_request-only trigger is drift rather than a file that is present and asleep; `tools/self-verify-drift-test.mjs` gains a case that strips the trigger from the shipped workflow and asserts `is missing the "on.push" key`, drift +1. Also here, found in review of this same change: both workflow steps now read `github.base_ref` and `github.event.before` through `env` instead of `${{ }}` interpolation, because a branch name is contributor-controlled text and the substitution happens before bash sees a quote.

Does not reproduce. The denial was fixed on 2026-08-04 by commit a196b2e ('stop pointing adopted repos at paths that only exist here'), after the round that recorded this finding, and it is proved closed here rather than assumed: running `standard/.claude/hooks/no-force-push.sh` with a PATH holding sed, awk and tr but no jq prints the real denial, and it names `https://github.com/repository-standards/core/blob/main/docs/method/prerequisites.md` - the by-reference form the rest of the tree uses, resolving to a file that exists in this repository. What was still true is that nothing held it closed: `link-check` resolves relative markdown links, and an absolute URL is skipped by construction, so all four instances of this class (the verifier's decisions line, this denial, an example claim in facts.example.json, and R16 citing a path as though it sat in the reader's repo) were found and swept by hand. `tools/link-check.mjs` now resolves every `https://github.com/repository-standards/core/blob|tree/main/<path>` link against the local tree, across every text file git knows about rather than only markdown - two of the four lived in a shell script and a JSON file. It finds 33 such links in the tree today and all resolve. Both edge cases were verified against a probe file rather than reasoned about: a URL ending a sentence (`.../prerequisites.md.`) resolves once trailing punctuation is stripped, a `<placeholder>` path is skipped as prose about the form, and a URL naming a path that is not here fails with the file and line.

Half of this had already closed and was checked rather than assumed: the shipped `standard/AGENTS.md` links both pages - `taxonomy.md` as the routing map and `checklist.md` as the decision catalog - added by commit 0240cc2 on 2026-08-04, hours before the round that recorded this finding as unresolved. The other named surface still reproduced: `standard/docs/conventions.md` linked `taxonomy.md` only, in a sentence that names both halves ('unsure which of these a given rule or fork is'), inside the file that exists to say where rules live. Both are linked now, from that same sentence. Verified by reading the shipped files rather than the rendered site. What is NOT claimed: nothing mechanical requires either link - a check for a link that is absent is a check for something that was never written, and the general form (does every by-reference URL resolve?) is closed under DOC-15 in the same pull request, which is a different question.
